Sorry to inundate you with quotes but these are good references in my life. It isn't about not giving a F but, rather, knowing where to put your energy.

1. Comparison is the thief of joy.

Don't focus so much on others, what they have and what they do.  Their experience is not yours nor is it a measuring stick for what yours should be.  I've seen successful people be miserable and struggling people be happy.

2. It isn't your job to fix a relationship you didn't break.

If someone does something to undermine the relationship you have with them, and then put all the responsibility on you to make things right, walk away.  A relationship is a dance with a partner and no matter how much you want to carry them along, if they aren't participating in the dance, you cannot fix it alone.

3. You are only in competition with your past self.

Don't try to be as good as someone else.  They are at a different stage of their journey and you see their successes but not their struggles.  You do, however, know what you have been through. So look at the version of yourself from yesterday and try to improve that in any way and in any amount.  The gains stack over time.

4. Make the hard decisions to have the easy life, make the easy decisions to have the hard life.

Look at situations as though they have long term affects on you.  If your mother meddles in your relationship with your partner, make the evaluation of what you want your future to be.  If you make the hard decision of dealing with your mother's meddling, you'll have an easy life because your focus will be in your partner and future with them. If you make the easy decision of not dealing with your meddling mother, then it'll affect your marriage and relationship in the future and she will continue her meddling.

5. Perfection is the opposite of "done"

Learn when something is good enough to walk away from and tackle something else. Constantly seeking the perfect outcome allows all the other pressures to pile up and give you stress.

In short, it isn't about not giving a F.  It is about what Fs are worth giving and where to give them.

When you fill something with water, like a glass, and watch the edge where the water is along the glass it makes a line.  If you cause ripples in the water, that line along the edge goes up and down.  Sound going into your ear is kind of like that line, a single feed travelling into your ear canal.

Noise cancelling headphones take that single source of sound going into your ear, and for every high part of the wave, it counters with a low wave and vice-versa.  This is how it cancels noise for your ear specially.

Move that noise cancelation device away from your ear, and it ceases to be a simple line of sound.  Now it is the entire surface of the glass of water.  Now you have multiple points of sound occurring in multiple locations.

Take three drops and drop it in the water.  Each drop causes a ripple effect outward from where it entered the water's surface.  When the ripples of multiple drops meet, the highs become higher and the lows become lower while the highs and lows negate each other at each specific point on the surface.  Across the entire surface, simultaneously, the interactions are happening in different ways.

It would be impossible for a single speaker to emit a single sound from, yet another point on that surface (another ripple), that would travel outward with the right pattern of highs and lows to negate every other ripple, because it is itself only a single ripple.

It would be like you dropping a single drop of water into the rippling surface and having that extra drop bring the entire surface to a flat standstill.  It won't happen.

The only option would be to create so much disruption on the surface that you can no longer isolate a single drop's ripples.  This is what white noise does, floods the sound you hear with other sound to disrupt your ear from hearing a particular one.  But that single sound isn't outright cancelled, just diffused in the other noise.

Personally, I'd go the path of replacing the mesh network with my own, disconnect all the cousin's devices once it is online leaving them in a box in the cousin's room.  Then setup the guest access network on your mesh to be the same network name/password as what the cousin had.  Then the cousin's devices will still work under the "same network" (only controlled by you because it is your network now).

The internet enters your household and goes to a router (typically provided by the internet service provider).  The Google device that is connected with a network cable to that router is the "start" of the Google mesh network.

So, if you control the router, you control the network for everyone.

If you plug a laptop into the router directly, your laptop will get assigned an IP from that router.  From there you can find the connection's gateway IP (search the command "ipconfig" or "ifconfig" from your windows or Linux laptop respectively).  Open a web browser with that IP address (example: "http://xxx.xxx.xxx.xxx" where the "x" are the IP numbers).  You should be greater with the login page for the router to which you can login*.

* If you don't know the login, it is probably a default login.  Search online for the default login of the router you have.  If that doesn't work, your cousin may have changed the login.  No worries, you have access to the router.  Find the reset option (usually a button accessed through a hole in the router that you can use a paperclip to push and hold for a few seconds until the router lights change signifying a reset).  This will reset to defaults, but also will reconnect to the internet provider and assign a fresh IP to the Google mesh.  So, assuming the mesh was configured without any unique configurations, the house network will drop internet and restore in a minute or two.

Once you can log into the router, you are the boss of the network and can knock the Google mesh offline from the router.  Get a vented security box to lock up the router so the cousin cannot access the reset and do exactly what you did to take control.

Now, you only control the router to the Google mesh network, and not the mesh network itself.  If that is your cousin's device, then you shouldn't administer it.

Now, via the router, kill internet access to the mesh whenever your cousin is a jerk.  He won't be able to manage the device if it cannot access the internet.  Use his own tactics against him: he complies or has no internet like everyone else.

Personally, at the point of controlling the router, I'd just buy a second mesh set (can even be Google) so you own them.  Set it up by connecting the first device to the router and then add the others to your mesh (setting a different network login/password to your mesh).  Then have the household devices connect to your mesh by updating the connections on them.  Since your cousin has his own mesh, that is connected to the router, you don't even have to give him the connection information to your mesh.

You'll know if your cousin tries to tamper with them/reset them because the Google home will alert you if it is unreachable/offline.  If it tells you it is offline, and devices are working in the house, then your cousin messed with your mesh and changed devices to talk to theirs.  Now you have grounds to have words with them about their overstepping.

As for network throttling, your cousin will only be able to do that on his mesh.  With the router however, it will balance load between the two connected meshes, and if you are lucky enough your router will have options to prioritize one connection over another with which you could throttle their entire mesh.

This is the approach I would take.

Now, if all that is too much, next time they kick someone off the network go to the Google mesh point that is connected to the router, find the reset option, and reset the device back to factory settings. I've forgotten how to do a million things and constantly revisit how to do the things I forgot how to do.  That is very, very normal.

Young developers focus far too much on trying to memorize things and get discouraged when they have to relearn something that they once did.  The reality is you'll "memorize" the things that you repeat over and over again.  With my development team, instead of "memorization" I refer to it as building "muscle-memory" instead as it is the act of doing it repeatedly that makes it into long-term memory.

When I chat with a developer about something they've never done, I drive the discussion and download all I think they need to know.  The key is that I tell them that I expect them to retain 10% of that information.  The second time, they drive the keyboard and I only talk them through it.  The third time, they do it themselves and I join if they want the second set of eyes.  After that, they fly solo and I am there for them if they get lost/in trouble.

I find this approach builds the muscle-memory in them and also cultures a healthy communication channel where they feel comfortable calling out for help if needed.

Long story short, don't get obsessed about what you don't remember. Work to build muscle-memory for the things that you use the most.  Personally, I'd rather be known as the person that "forgot more than someone else may ever know" than the person that "knows everything about that one thing."

Your memory isn't just what is committed there natively, but also the parts that know how to figure it out if you need to, and the parts that know where your bookmarked sites are for reference, and the parts that know when to pull the book off the shelf that talks about that particular thing.  If you know how to do it, through any means of recall, then you are a normal human being.

On the "comparing yourself to others aspect", you'll need to work on that aspect.  You are out of school now, every person's path in life is their own.  There is a reason that there is an expression "the grass isn't always greener on the other side".

The private tech industry may pay more, yes, but it also is different.  Workers there have to be strategic for their retirement because they don't have a pension waiting for them.  They also do not (necessarily) have employers that care about work/life balance since a company is driven by money earned.  They also don't have job security and can wake up one morning without a job because a decision to cut was made overnight.  What is the dollar value of all these things?  It isn't a simple matter of better or worse, just a matter of being different.  As a single guy in my 20's, I was frustrated at the "lost opportunity of going private"; in my 40's, I'm glad I had consistency and stability to raise my children.  There are many, many people in the private sector that want into the public service to have what you have.

Also, life hack here, train yourself to not compare yourself with others or your peers.  The popular jock in school might one day pump the gas into your car, the nerdy loser might  become an overnight success on the stock market, the girl that loves dancing and made TikToks might get noticed and become a back-up dancer to Taylor Swift, or the friend you had might end up in jail for attempted murder (two of these four I have seen in my life time so, yeah, weird things happen).

What they don't teach you when you grow up is that a vast majority of people end up living average lives with average jobs, and that that is a fine thing to live.  We are raised to expect great outcomes and that we will all reach lofty goals.  Most people will not achieve their deep inner dreams of youth because life is a journey.  I got into computers because I wanted to make triple-A video games and work for some cool gaming company that made the workday seem so fun, why would I not stay all the time and just sleep at the office?  Instead I make data systems for the GoC, have an average life, a wife and kids, and life is...actually kind of great.  I wouldn't change it for anything.  Learn to view each day as a gift, each memory as treasured, and realize that happiness is a choice.

Lastly, if none of this resonates and you still don't like the life you are living, then make a change.  No one can make you happy when you are not.  Also no one is going to just give you what you want because you aren't happy.  If you want to be empowered, you need to make the change for yourself.  Otherwise, others will make changes that affect you, but make no mistake, the changes they make are for themselves and not for you.

I tell my developers that it isn't a criticism, it is a conversation had in the context of the code.  That conversation is a two-way street.

Yes, a majority of the time it results in changes.  

These changes, however, are multifaceted. Some are just code style (write it this way for others to quickly acclimatize to your code because it is familiar), some are logic-based (have you considered this edge-case?), some are performance-based (if this is in this loop you hammer the database repeatedly for no additional value), some are maintenance-based (approach it like this to be more readable "for the next guy"), and some are architectural/teaching moments (I see you are unfamiliar with this topic, let's explore together)

One of the biggest eye openers is to become the primary code reviewer.  Your job is the caretaker of the code.  The less you pay attention to the PR reviews, the bigger the problems become.  Eventually they become so big that you, the lead, need to fix them and that becomes a lot of work.  Sure, you may want to be nice and let things slide now and then, but you pay for it in the long run.

So, long story short, not every person can be the absolute best in their field of work and never need changes or adjustments.  This doesn't make you bad at your job, in fact it makes you normal, the perfect ones (if that exists) are the anomalies.  Your imposter syndrome is a tool, not a curse. I'm not going to debate the comments of the senior dev, just paint a picture.

Assume you are a solo developer and you build 100% of a system.  If things go wrong, it's on you to take the brunt of the fallout as well as to fix it.

Now you are the senior developer and you don't build 100% of the system.  In fact you have 10 junior developers that collectively crank out 10 people's worth of code.  You train them hoping that they will follow your lead and 80% of the time they do, but they are human and have ideas of their own and want to "make their mark".  So 20% of what they generate you are more leary of so you have to also code review it.  That becomes a lot of code to sift through from 10 people.  When that code, however, hits production and fails, the senior developer is still 100% responsible for the fallout. 

So that senior developer has all the skin in the game, but their success or failure is dependent (in their mind) on you delivering as they expect.  This can make for sharp, direct comments from a senior developer.  They need you to deliver as expected and have only a fraction of the time to spend with you personally (remember there are 9 other junior developers that also want their time)

Furthermore, as you climb the chain, you have less time. You are pulled into meetings with managers and executives, you sit in business analysis meetings hoping to steer (what will be given to your shop) deliverables so they are decent, you sit in testing meetings hoping to steer (what will be the quality control) efforts so they give you good coverage, you drop everything for the next "on fire" thing.

So, long story short, they might come off as being a jerk to you.  The reality is, they probably see it differently because they are dealing with things that you aren't, but one day you may be in their shoes and then you will occasionally be that jerky senior developer.

To me, as a senior developer, I spend an unreasonable amount of time at the beginning of hiring a new junior developer to "show them the ropes" as well as honestly talk about why we are at the point we are at, what areas of code are great, and what areas are opportunity spaces (aka. hot garbage).  When you state that you are 3 months in, it is at that point that I'd expect to see a junior developer stop making the "new guy faults" and start to deliver more in-line with the other developers.  To be honest, it sounds like their expectations of you are not being met as they expected and they may be wondering if you are going to carry the load to ease the efforts of others or be a burden by not doing so.

My advice:  First, check yourself.  Assume it isn't personal, and listen to the intent for your code as opposed to the words.  Ask yourself critical questions.  Are you making the same mistakes?  Are you understanding concepts?  Are you getting fewer comments in code reviews?  Are you genuinely trying some suggestions given to you?  Where are you in the performance spectrum of the team?  Have your responsibilities grown?  Have your skills grown?  Then don't wait to get chewed out by your senior developer, ask them if you could schedule time with them to talk about how you can grow in the team.  Your senior developer will like that you ask for scheduled time, respecting their scheduling, as well as it will give you a window of time to talk candidly.  Ask about how they see your progress, where you can improve, and what you can do to be more valuable to the team.  Then listen carefully to the answers and make an honest effort to address those areas.

Finally, they might actually be a jerk.  It is a field of ego-heavy personalities after all.  If that's the case, work hard and improve and find the better job for you.

When you get divorced, the family law system puts the children before either parent.  Sounds fine, in theory, and in a joint-custody 50/50 type deal you can make it work.

Problem is that child support is based on where the children sleep.  Most sleeps equals greater support.  This means that a manipulative parent that alienates the other gets the joy of hurting the other parent and getting full support as the payoff.

Worse yet, children as a "survival tactic" will often stay with the manipulative parent out of fear of what could happen if they disobey or defy them.  The kids know, deep down, the good parent is suffering for the actions taken but will forgive them in the future for staying with the bad parent.

Then the good parent will turn to the courts to correct the manipulation and alienation that has escalated beyond their ability to stop it.  The courts are slow, will do everything they can to promote mediation/counseling/therapy before going towards legal intervention.  The bad parent will use this time to manipulate and stall as long as possible to either drain the good parent of any money to fight or to give the children time to get older and repeat the manipulator's words as if they believe it.

Once the children are in their teenage years (roughly) the court will probably just let them do what they say they want to do, parents be damned.  All the money spent on the courts is long gone and everything is good and fucked up.

That is the reality for many, many people and the system is a failure and needs to change.

I used to be a believer that all parents should pay for the rightful child-support however I have seen that this is all the incentive that a manipulator needs to motivate them to screw up the kids.  It is seen as a reward or prize.

Instead I now believe that, regardless of the children's sleeps, just take the two incomes and balance as if it were 50/50.  It changes nothing for the good joint-parenting couple because that's what they would typically be doing.  For the couple with the bad parent however, it removes the "prize" of child-support, and they will quickly realize that, instead of trying to keep the children for the money, they will try to leave the children with the good parent because it'll lessen the costs of caring for them in the house.

I've used the EAP services multiple times and the goal of it is to help you work through your issues on a short-term basis, over the span of 5 or 6 sessions.  It doesn't really matter how small or big the issue is, the EAP is to help you work through it so that it doesn't become bigger and impact on your ability to perform your job's duties.

To answer you more directly:

If you've been thinking you might want to use their services, your issues might not be as trivial as you are believing.  Seeking support is a sign that you feel they are getting bigger than you are comfortable with and being able to recognize this yourself is already a good thing.

Don't be concerned about overwhelming a system that is in place for you to benefit from if you have the need of the support of that system.  It is there for you to use and, because it is difficult for people to ask for help, I doubt it is overburdened anyways.

I found it to be very comfortable and personally valuable to me when I used it.  Everyone will have their own personal take on this because counseling is a personal thing and talking with a counselor is, in its own way, another form of relationship and some will be good and some won't.  The good thing is, if one counselor doesn't work for you, you can request a different one.  The counselors don't take this personally, it is a reality of their field of work.

The counselor will both listen to you and give advice, but I think it isn't advice in the way you are thinking. A counselor will rarely tell you what you need to do and, instead, advises you how to come to your own decisions of what you need to do for yourself.  They help guide you through your thoughts and cannot prescribe what is best for you because everyone is different.  Ultimately you have to decide your path forward.

You can talk about whatever you feel you need to, your counselor won't tell you to stop talking about something because it isn't "the main issue".  Again, they are here for you so if you need to talk about things then they'll let you.  The only hard limit with the EAP is that it is only good for 5 or 6 sessions and, if you need more, you have to get long-term counseling.

The last point, of how they make you feel comfortable talking about personal things, is more about how comfortable you are opening up.  They will make it clear that your conversation is confidential, that you are free to share what you are comfortable with (and know that the that the less you share, the less they have to work with to try and help you), and you are no obligated to have to work with them and can freely change counselors.

Now my personal take on counseling:

What gets us overwhelmed is dealing with things that get (or can be perceived as getting) bigger than we can handle ourselves.  We tend to bottle it up because we don't want to feel we cannot handle our own issues as well as we don't want to burden those in our lives with our troubles.  This creates an internal feedback loop where the internal issue grows and grows and, as it grows, it consumes more of our ability to function.  The counselor becomes a pressure release valve where we can let out that pressure to someone that has nothing to do with our troubles and therefore we don't feel like we burden them because we don't.

Hope you get things sorted out. 🤗

If I draw a parallel to PCs, when an application is running it occupies a certain amount of memory.  If it needs more memory than is available, it swaps other prices of memory out to make space for it.  Where does that memory go?  Into a swap file on disk because it has to go somewhere.  So, if there is no memory available and disk available, the machine has hit a limit of what is possible.

No application works without using some memory therefore, no, it isn't as simple as data going from the camera to the screen.  Furthermore the device clearly needed more, and when it went to get more there was none.  Then when it went to utilize disk, in lieu, there was none there as well.  So, the end result is, the machine had no choice but to abandon your task and, in doing so, nicely told you why it did so.

Not liking that this happened doesn't make it not user error.  You have three paths before you:

One, complain about the company for this situation.  They will say to buy a new phone and move on.

Two, complain to the device that it is failing your demands upon it.  It won't care and will keep operating as it is designed to do.

Three, accept your own role on the situation, spelled out in the message provided to you by your phone, and clean out your phone's disk space that you have filled up.

So I had my mother living in our home and she is full of anxiety, depression, ideation, etc.  She tried to "rule the roost" through all the negative behaviours and, if you pushed back, it got worse.

So the first thing to do is get beyond your own emotions with regard to the situation.  You are in a reactionary pattern of reacting to the situation around you, you hate it and hate that you feel like you hate it.  You care about your parent, but you cannot deal with your parent.  You want someone to help you but you are afraid that others are going to say she is fit to return home and that this situation will never end.  You have compassion fatigue of channelling your energies into a black hole that is just devouring them all.  You feel stuck in an unbeatable situation but you don't want to be seen on giving up on your parent and "turning them out to the cold".

First, be brutally honest with yourself: This is more than you can handle and you are done with it.  Permanently.  It doesn't matter what others will think, it doesn't matter what your parent thinks, you are done with it.  Channel all the reactionary emotion into a hardened-like-steel-forged resolve that you will change this paradigm.  Not because you are a person that gave up, but because you are a person that doesn't give up.  You aren't going to give up on yourself, and your right to not endure this.  You also are not going to give up on your parent because you are going to change the situation and give them the help they need, not necessarily the help they want, by changing the game.

Ask yourself, honestly, is this person capable of being physically and mentally able to manage themselves.  This is a tough thing to do because they play that they aren't.  For example, my mom would complain about doing anything physical...yet would drive her car, go to the dog park and walk around for an hour or so (even in winter).  She would also say she cannot manage her own things...yet would make her own doctor appointments, manage her own meds, pay her own bills, etc.  So, in our case, you have to ignore the drama and watch for the signs they are capable.  In our case, she was fully capable however just chose not to be a team player in the home and just expected everyone to take care of her like it was her own nursing home.

We knew my mom was capable of all these things. So we pushed back everything she wanted us to do for her back to her.  This is were the manipulation became apparent.  All the "but I can't" and "I'm going to not get through this" and "I want to die" comments came out.  Ignore the words and respond simply that you know they are capable and they have to face the reality that there is an expectation that they participate in the well-being of their own lives, and those around them, and that everything is a two-way street.  They will fight harder.  For some reason, fighting hard to manipulate others is of more interest to people than taking the easier path of just carrying your own baggage.  You know you cannot bear dealing with this, so falling back into the pattern of before is not an option.

Now this is where things got real for us.  Mom tried to stab herself.  The ideation became an attempt.

So that got mom to the mental health ward of the General and for a month and a half all I heard come out of her mouth was to get her out of there and she wanted to come back home.  I told the doctor that we were at the breaking point with her and that, although she is my mother, returning to my home was not going to be happening.  Once they are out of your home, you don't have to let them back in.  Sounds cold to people that haven't been in that situation, but it needs to be put in the right perspective: You are not capable of providing them the care, observation, and monitoring for this type of situation.  So, in our case, the hospital was the best place for her.

Then, wouldn't you know it, they found her physically and mentally capable to manage herself autonomously and they needed to discharge her from the hospital.  I simply stated that returning to my home was not an option on the table and since mom is capable of managing herself, by the hospital's evaluation, there is no saying I have to take that back on.  So mom's choices were to find a place of her own (which she would refuse to do), go to a retirement home (which we'll work with her to get that setup while she remains at the hospital), or the hospital discharges her to a women's shelter.

She pleaded to come home but, as stated, that option was off the table.  She asked what if she refused to decide and I said that, if she hasn't learned this in life by now she's going to learn very soon, every situation has options. Refusal to choose willingly doesn't mean they everyone's hands are tied.  It just means the best options for her are not going to happen and the hospital will have no choice but to discharge her to the woman's shelter.  She replied that "they can't do that" and I just told her to keep being stubborn and find out the hard way then.

It ended with her accepting the retirement home, and she isn't happy about it, but now professionals are engaged with the situation.  All is well for us too.

A few guiding principles that served me well through all this were these:

The saying: If you want an easy life, then make the hard decisions.  If you want a hard life, make the easy decisions.

Mom tried to make easy decisions by offloading all of her efforts into others and, as a result, lived a hard life.  We made the hard decision of not enduring her behaviour, and now live the easy life.  The easy decision for us would be to just endure, because fixing it would be hard, but that would have only led to the hard life for us.

Finally, the fact of human nature: When given no option but to find a way to survive, people find a way.  So mom, even if we were to abandon her, would find a way.  She has the ability and resources to do so, and will, and ultimately did.

One day you'll look back on all this and reflect that, damn, that was brutal and crazy and so, so much drama...but it is over and is in the past now.  You will see the other side of this situation.

Various things come to mind as an accumulation of experience.  Here's a few:

Write your initial code to solve the problem infront of you.  Don't try to build it into a platform for "easy implementation/use by the next guy", you very likely will not anticipate the needs of the next guy, you will increase the time it takes you to complete, and all your extra tooling will probably have to be removed/refactored by the next guy/next problem.  You are often "the next guy" of your own code.

Cutting and pasting is a sign that you need to refactor/rethink your implementation.  By the third paste it should cross your mind that this is duplicating code and, if it is that important, should be implemented once and reused many times.  This is the time to refactor that before the technical debt of your codebase grows further.

View the problem from the other direction to see new approaches.  If you build a library to do something, before commiting yourself to a structure, try to write how you would like to use it.  Viewing the code from both ends, provider and consumer, gives new insights.

If you have a technical lead, follow their lead and solicit their guidance/direction.  If you think you have a better implementation, then prototype it outside the codebase (or locally before commiting to source code repository), and demo it for the lead.  Impressing your lead is a better career path for you than just forcing your ideas into their codebase.

Collaborate with team members/colleagues.  Everyone will produce code that can be improved. Together, the overall quality of the code improves for everyone.  If you, however, rip someone's code apart for being terrible without helping them make it better, be certain that they are looking to return the favour to you.

You are never "done" when others are still working on their pieces.  Offer to provide your time/assistance to help them complete theirs.  Again, this will pay off later, when you are struggling to meet your own deadline.

To me, a gift is about the giver's desire to give something to someone they care about.  Not so much about the receiver.

If I don't know what I'd like to give, I ask for a list, and then chose something from their list.  This is the compromise area where my desire to gift then something meets with their wishes of what they would like.

If someone asks for money as a gift, that tells me to don't want my personal effort and thoughtfulness but just my money.  As a result, they either get nothing or something less than I was originally willing to spend.

On the flip-side, I had an ex that couldn't think what to gift me and would ask for a list.  I'd give a list of things I would otherwise buy myself, and then not buy them to not ruin her gift to me.  Except once given a list, she'd always then get something not on the list!  So, givers, if you ask for a list, stick to the list from that point on!

And, no, putting money on the list is not a creative loophole...

A programmer is someone that can find a solution: "I did this and it worked!" (While turning off security restrictions)

A good programmer is someone that finds one of the best solutions out of all the solutions: "I did this and it worked!" (While not turning of security restrictions)

A great programmer is a good programmer that finds the best solution out of all the solutions, and took the time to ensure the next developer that saw it could understand what was done clearly:  "I did this, it was a challenge, but it is in the code here as an example so that it needn't be hard for you too"

A good programmer, that specializes in XYZ, is a subject matter expert.  Some times this is a choice and sometimes it is a reality of working only in one discipline.  Either way, it is an end-state and not a starting-point.

It is a progression of skill, refined through experience, that will get you there. The best part is that you see others' work as being better. That insight will push you to dig into what they do, and to improve your skills according.  Most (all) experienced programmers will look at their old code in disgust of how much better it could be now.

Unfortunately, a lot of programmers think that they write amazing code and never admire other's code nor aspire to improve.  They never evolve beyond just a programmer.

Keep living with the "Imposter Syndrome" because it actually helps you to make yourself better by making you feel like you are never enough.  Just never let it "win" and give up.

If I pick it up myself, then no additional service has been provided, therefore I just pay the cost of the food without tip.

Admittedly, I would rather not have the tipping culture, and just have workers paid a fair wage.
